It is wearing plate armour and it is charging. Walrus Audio’s illustrators have never been subtle about announcing what a box is for, and the Ages announces something specific: this is not a delicate, transparent, get-out-of-the-way overdrive. This is a thing that arrives with weight behind it. GG-ARTICLE-AFTER-INTRO The Walrus Audio Ages Five-State Overdrive landed in May 2020 and it landed with a confession attached. “We haven’t released an overdrive since 2016,” Walrus wrote on the product page, “and with there being more overdrives out there than stars in the sky, we didn’t want to create another one unless we thought it was important.” That is a company from Oklahoma City admitting, in public, that the overdrive market is saturated to the point of absurdity — and then releasing an overdrive anyway. The Ages is the argument for why they bothered. The pitch has three legs. Five internally switched gain-and-clipping states on a rotary knob. A dry blend control that runs a parallel clean path alongside the drive. And a bass control wired before the gain stage rather than after it. Individually, none of those is unheard of. Together, in one enclosure, at a street price that started at $199, they add up to a pedal that behaves less like a single overdrive and more like a small cabinet of them. Dave Hunter reviewed it for Premier Guitar in September 2020 and closed with a line that has followed the pedal around ever since: “chances are, you’ll pick a setting, play it, and smile.” That is both a compliment and, if you read it a certain way, the pedal’s central problem. We will get to both. How to Get the Tone ↓ The Four-Year Silence: Why Walrus Waited Walrus Audio started building pedals in Oklahoma City in 2011. By the middle of the 2010s the company had a reputation built almost entirely on ambience and modulation — the Julia chorus, the Descent reverb, the ARP-87 delay. Dirt was a smaller part of the story: the Iron Horse LM308 distortion arrived in 2012, the Voyager preamp/overdrive and the 385 followed, and then the drive catalogue simply stopped growing. Four years is a long time in the pedal industry, and it is a particularly long time in overdrive, where the release cycle is relentless and mostly consists of Tube Screamer variations with different names.
